summary.text: For one-digit \(n\), \(10n\) is an explicit distinct partner. For \(n\ge10\), the proof constructs a multiple \(k\) of \(D(n)\) with \(D(k)=n\): after removing the factors \(2\) and \(5\) from \(D(n)\), it uses \(n\equiv D(n)\pmod 9\), a solvable congruence \(n+9y\equiv0\), and digit blocks spaced by an Euler-totient period, then appends zeros to restore those factors; finally \(D(n)<n\) ensures \(k\ne n\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(r)\) denote the sum of the ordinary base-10 digits of a nonnegative integer \(r\). We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has a positive integer \(k\ne n\) such that
\[
D(n)\mid k\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
This makes the set from which \(a(n)\) is chosen nonempty. Since every member of that set is positive, its least member is positive, and hence \(a(n)\ne0\).

We first record some elementary facts about decimal digit sums.

1. If \(r>0\), then \(D(r)>0\).
2. For every \(r\), \(D(r)\le r\).
3. If \(r\ge10\), then in fact \(D(r)<r\).
4. One has
\[
D(r)\equiv r\pmod 9.
\]

The first assertion is immediate because the decimal expansion of a positive integer has a nonzero digit. For the second and third, write \(r=10q+u\), where \(0\le u<10\). If \(r>0\), then \(D(r)=D(q)+u\). Induction on the number of digits gives \(D(q)\le q\), and therefore \(D(r)\le q+u\le10q+u=r\). If \(r\ge10\), then \(q>0\), so \(q+u<10q+u\), proving strict inequality. The congruence modulo \(9\) follows from \(10^i\equiv1\pmod9\): an integer and the sum of its decimal digits have the same residue modulo \(9\).

A consequence that will be important below is
\[
\gcd(D(r),9)\mid r. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the gcd divides both \(D(r)\) and \(9\), and the congruence \(r\equiv D(r)\pmod9\) then implies that it divides \(r\).

We now prove the main auxiliary existence result.

**Digit-sum divisibility lemma.** Suppose \(s,m\) are positive integers satisfying
\[
m\le s\qquad\text{and}\qquad \gcd(m,9)\mid s.
\]
Then there exists a positive integer \(K\) such that
\[
D(K)=s\qquad\text{and}\qquad m\mid K. \tag{2}
\]

We first prove this when \(\gcd(10,m)=1\).

The congruence
\[
9y+s\equiv0\pmod m \tag{3}
\]
has a solution, because a linear congruence \(9y\equiv-s\pmod m\) is solvable exactly when \(\gcd(9,m)\mid s\). Choose its least nonnegative solution, so that
\[
0\le y<m.
\]
For completeness, this standard solvability statement can be seen by putting \(g=\gcd(9,m)\). Since \(g\mid s\), write \(9=g\alpha\), \(m=g\beta\), and \(s=g\sigma\). Then \(\gcd(\alpha,\beta)=1\), so \(\alpha\) has a multiplicative inverse modulo \(\beta\). Thus one may solve \(\alpha y\equiv-\sigma\pmod\beta\); this is equivalent to \(9y+s\equiv0\pmod m\). Reducing a solution modulo \(m\) gives one in the stated range.

There is one special case. Suppose \(m\mid9\). The hypothesis \(\gcd(m,9)\mid s\) then says \(m\mid s\). Let \(K\) be the number consisting of \(s\) consecutive digits equal to \(1\):
\[
K=1+10+10^2+\cdots+10^{s-1}.
\]
Its digit sum is \(s\). Moreover, \(m\mid9\) gives \(10\equiv1\pmod m\), and hence
\[
K\equiv s\equiv0\pmod m.
\]
Thus (2) holds in this case.

We may therefore assume that \(m\nmid9\). Let
\[
\lambda=\varphi(m).
\]
Since \(m>0\), \(\varphi(m)>0\). In fact \(\lambda>1\): the only positive integers having totient \(1\) are \(1\) and \(2\); the first divides \(9\), while the second is not coprime to \(10\). Euler's theorem gives
\[
10^\lambda\equiv1\pmod m. \tag{4}
\]

Because \(y<m\le s\), we have \(y\le s\). Set
\[
x=s-y.
\]
We next represent both \(x\) and \(y\) as sums of decimal digits. For any nonnegative integer \(t\), define a finite digit list \(R(t)\) by taking \(\lfloor t/9\rfloor\) copies of the digit \(9\), followed, if nonzero, by the remainder \(t\bmod9\). Every entry of \(R(t)\) lies between \(0\) and \(9\), and
\[
\sum_{a\in R(t)}a
=9\left\lfloor\frac t9\right\rfloor+(t\bmod9)=t. \tag{5}
\]
Write
\[
A=R(x)=(A_0,A_1,\ldots),\qquad B=R(y)=(B_0,B_1,\ldots),
\]
extending both finite lists by zeros after their ends.

We construct \(K\) by placing the digits of \(A\) in decimal positions congruent to \(0\pmod\lambda\), and the digits of \(B\) in positions congruent to \(1\pmod\lambda\). Explicitly,
\[
K=\sum_{j\ge0} A_j10^{j\lambda}
  +\sum_{j\ge0} B_j10^{j\lambda+1}. \tag{6}
\]
Both sums are finite. Since \(\lambda>1\), the positions \(j\lambda\) and \(j\lambda+1\) are all distinct: two positions within either family are distinct, and a position from the first family cannot equal one from the second because their residues modulo \(\lambda\) are different. Thus (6) is genuinely a decimal expansion with digits drawn from the two lists and with zeros in all unused positions; there are no carries. Consequently, by (5),
\[
D(K)=\sum_j A_j+\sum_j B_j=x+y=s. \tag{7}
\]

Modulo \(m\), equation (4) gives
\[
10^{j\lambda}\equiv1,
\qquad
10^{j\lambda+1}\equiv10.
\]
Using (5) once more in (6), we obtain
\[
K\equiv \sum_j A_j+10\sum_j B_j
=x+10y
=(s-y)+10y
=s+9y
\equiv0\pmod m
\]
by the choice of \(y\) in (3). Hence \(m\mid K\), and (7) gives the required digit sum. This completes the proof of the auxiliary lemma when \(m\) is coprime to \(10\).

We now remove that coprimality assumption. Factor out the complete powers of \(2\) and \(5\) from \(m\): write
\[
m=2^a5^b m',
\]
where \(a\) and \(b\) are respectively the largest exponents for which \(2^a\mid m\) and \(5^b\mid m\). Then \(m'>0\) and neither \(2\) nor \(5\) divides \(m'\), so
\[
\gcd(10,m')=1. \tag{8}
\]
Also \(2^a5^b\) is coprime to \(9\), and therefore removing this factor does not change the gcd with \(9\):
\[
\gcd(m',9)=\gcd(m,9). \tag{9}
\]
Thus \(\gcd(m',9)\mid s\). Moreover \(m'\le m\le s\). By the coprime case already proved, there is an integer \(K'>0\) such that
\[
D(K')=s,
\qquad
m'\mid K'. \tag{10}
\]
The positivity follows in any event from \(D(K')=s>0\).

Let \(t=\max(a,b)\), and define
\[
K=K'10^t.
\]
Multiplication by \(10^t\) merely appends \(t\) zeros to the decimal expansion, so
\[
D(K)=D(K')=s. \tag{11}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
10^t=2^t5^t

automatically contains the factors \(2^a\) and \(5^b\), since \(t\ge a,b\). Hence \(2^a5^b\mid10^t\). Combining this with \(m'\mid K'\) gives
\[
m=m'2^a5^b\mid K'10^t=K.
\]
Equations (11) and this divisibility prove the digit-sum divisibility lemma in full generality.

We apply the lemma to construct a Harshad amicable partner of an arbitrary positive integer \(n\). There are two cases.

**Case 1: \(1\le n<10\).** Then \(D(n)=n\). Take
\[
k=10n.
\]
This is positive and is distinct from \(n\), since \(n>0\). Its decimal expansion is that of \(n\) followed by a zero, so
\[
D(k)=D(n)=n.
\]
Therefore
\[
D(n)=n\mid10n=k,
\qquad
D(k)=n\mid n.
\]
Thus \(k\) is a partner of \(n\).

**Case 2: \(n\ge10\).** Put
\[
m=D(n),\qquad s=n.
\]
The preliminary digit-sum facts show that \(m>0\) and \(m\le n=s\). By (1),
\[
\gcd(m,9)=\gcd(D(n),9)\mid n=s.
\]
The digit-sum divisibility lemma therefore supplies an integer \(k\) satisfying
\[
D(k)=n,
\qquad
D(n)=m\mid k. \tag{12}
\]
Since \(D(k)=n>0\), the integer \(k\) is positive. Also (12) immediately gives \(D(k)\mid n\), because in fact \(D(k)=n\). It remains only to check that \(k\ne n\). If \(k=n\), then (12) would imply
\[
D(n)=n.
\]
But for \(n\ge10\) we proved the strict inequality \(D(n)<n\), a contradiction. Thus \(k\ne n\), and \(k\) is again a partner of \(n\).

We have proved in all cases that the set
\[
P_n=\{k\in\mathbb N: k>0,\ k\ne n,\ D(n)\mid k,\ D(k)\mid n\}
\]
is nonempty whenever \(n>0\). Every nonempty set of natural numbers has a least element, and every element of \(P_n\) is positive. By definition, \(a(n)\) is this least element when \(P_n\) is nonempty (and is defined as \(0\) only when it is empty). Therefore, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
a(n)>0,
\]
and in particular \(a(n)\ne0\), as claimed.
